title: Capitolo 1 · Alphabet, introductions, numbers and the classroom
shortDescription: Your first steps in Italian: the alphabet and pronunciation, greetings, introducing yourself with "essere", numbers 0–20 and your age with "avere", and the objects and instructions of the classroom.
description:
Part of the official SS Europa Italian course used in our classes, for learners from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh who are going to Italy to work, study or live. Chapters 1–7 take you from zero to level A1 and Chapters 8–12 to level A2 — study them in order.

Every 60-minute class of the chapter is split into three short lessons you can study on your phone, with pictures, audio, grammar tables and exercises. Every word comes with its English and Punjabi meaning, the slides of each class are attached as PDF, and the chapter ends with a test (pass mark 60%).
objectives:
I can say the Italian alphabet and spell my name
I can pronounce C and G correctly (ciao / casa, gelato / gatto)
I can greet people formally and informally and use polite words
I can say my name, city and nationality and ask other people
I can count from 0 to 20 and say my age and phone number
I can name classroom objects with un / uno / una / un' and understand the teacher's instructions

lessons.title: Lesson 1 · The Italian alphabet
lessons.summary: The 21 Italian letters, how to say them and one word for each letter.

blocks.title: Class slides: Capitolo 1 · Lezione 1 (PDF)
blocks.body: The slides your teacher uses in class. Open them on your phone or print them.

blocks.title: Le 21 lettere italiane
blocks.body:
The Italian alphabet has **21 letters**: A B C D E F G H I L M N O P Q R S T U V Z.

The letters **J, K, W, X, Y** are "foreign letters" (lettere straniere). They are used only in foreign words such as *jeans*, *kiwi*, *web*, *taxi*, *yoga*.

The 5 vowels (vocali) are **A, E, I, O, U**. In Italian every vowel is always pronounced, and always in the same way.

blocks.title: Good to know
blocks.body: A vowel with an accent at the end of a word (**città, caffè, sì, però, più**) is said **strong and clear**, with the voice on the last syllable. The accent can change the meaning: **si** (oneself) / **sì** (yes).

lessons.title: Lesson 1 · Pronunciation: C and G
lessons.summary: Soft and hard C and G: ciao or casa? gelato or gatto?

blocks.title: La lettera C: suono dolce e suono duro
blocks.body:
**C** has two sounds:

- **Soft [ch]** like *church* (Punjabi "ch", chacha) before **E** and **I**: **ce, ci** — and **cia, cio, ciu**.
- **Hard [k]** like *cat* (Punjabi "k", kakka) before **A, O, U**: **ca, co, cu** — and **che, chi** (the H makes it hard).

blocks.title: La lettera G: suono dolce e suono duro
blocks.body:
**G** works the same way:

- **Soft [j]** like *gel* (Punjabi "j", jajja): **ge, gi** — and **gia, gio, giu**.
- **Hard [g]** like *go* (Punjabi "g", gagga): **ga, go, gu** — and **ghe, ghi**.

blocks.title: Good to know
blocks.body: Remember the trick: **H after C or G makes the sound hard** (chiave, spaghetti). **I after C or G makes it soft** (ciao, giorno) and the I is almost not heard.

blocks.body: In Italy you greet everyone when you walk into a shop or an office: **Buongiorno** in the morning, **Buonasera** from the afternoon. **Ciao** is only for friends, family and children. With people you don't know say **Salve** or **Buongiorno**.

blocks.title: Adesso tocca a te! (Now it's your turn)
blocks.body:
1. **Ciao / Buongiorno!** — greet your partner
2. **Mi chiamo… Come ti chiami?** — say your name (Apna naam dasso)
3. **Sono di… / Sono… Di dove sei?** — say your city and nationality (Shahir ate desh dasso)

lessons.title: Lesson 3 · How old are you? The verb "avere"
lessons.titleIt: Lezione 3 · Quanti anni hai? Il verbo avere
lessons.summary: Io ho, tu hai, lui/lei ha — and how Italians say their age.

blocks.title: Il verbo AVERE (to have · H muta!)

blocks.body:
The **H** of *ho, hai, ha* is silent (muta): **ho** sounds like "o", **ha** like "a".

In Italian you **have** years: *Ho 20 anni* = I am 20 (literally "I have 20 years"). Punjabi: *Meri umar 20 saal hai*.

items.punjabi: Aap ji di umar kinni hai?

blocks.title: Good to know
blocks.body: Never say "Sono 20 anni" — that is wrong. Use **avere**: **Ho 20 anni.**

blocks.title: Good to know
blocks.body: Phone numbers are read **digit by digit** or in small groups: *tre-quattro-otto, dodici, zero-nove…*. In Italy mobile numbers always start with **3** (320, 333, 347, 389…).

lessons.title: Lesson 4 · Masculine, feminine and un / uno / una / un'
lessons.titleIt: Lezione 4 · Maschile, femminile e articoli indeterminativi
lessons.summary: Nouns in -o and -a, and how to say "a / an" in Italian.

blocks.title: Maschile (-O) e femminile (-A)
blocks.body:
Every Italian noun is **masculine** or **feminine**.

- **Masculine** nouns usually end in **-O**: libro, quaderno, tavolo (Pulling: akkhar -O naal khatam hunda hai)
- **Feminine** nouns usually end in **-A**: penna, sedia, lavagna (Istriling: akkhar -A naal khatam hunda hai)

blocks.title: Articoli indeterminativi (a / an · Ikk)
table: un libro · un tavolo · un banco

blocks.title: Good to know
blocks.body: **Un'** with the apostrophe is only for **feminine** words that start with a vowel (un'aula). Masculine words with a vowel take **un** without apostrophe: *un amico, un orologio*.

lessons.homework: Write 8 classroom objects with the right article: un…, uno…, una…, un'….

blocks.title: Le istruzioni in classe (one student / the whole class)

blocks.body: The form in **-a / -i** (ascolta, leggi) is for **one** student. The form in **-ate / -ete** (ascoltate, leggete) is for the **whole class**.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 test
lessons.summary: Listening, vocabulary, numbers, essere / avere and articles. Pass mark: 60%.

blocks.title: Test Capitolo 1
blocks.body:
This test checks everything in Chapter 1: alphabet and pronunciation, greetings, introducing yourself (essere / avere), numbers 0–20 and classroom objects.

- **1. Listening** — listen and choose the word or number
- **2. Vocabulary and greetings**
- **3. Grammar** — essere, avere and un / uno / una / un'
- **4. Writing** — build sentences to introduce yourself

You need **60%** to pass. You can repeat the test as many times as you like.

blocks.title: Good to know
blocks.body: The **oral interview** (greeting and name, spelling your name, city and age — 2 minutes) and the written presentation are done **with your teacher** in the live class.
